name: Protein supplements in older adults
short: A review cautions long-term high dietary protein in older age and/or CKD may worsen kidney function. Supplement reviews in older adults: no serious adverse events in one, stomach upset in another.
text: In a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials in 1,057 adults aged 65 or over with sarcopenia or physical frailty, no serious adverse events were reported with protein supplementation, and in a meta-analysis of 55 trials of oral protein and energy supplements in older people, ten trials reported gastrointestinal disturbances such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. The kidney evidence in the cited sources concerns total dietary protein intake or higher-protein diets rather than supplements specifically. A meta-analysis of 28 trials in adults without kidney disease (not limited to older adults) found that the change in kidney filtration rate did not differ between higher- and lower-protein diets. In contrast, a review concluded that long-term high dietary protein intake in individuals of older age and/or with CKD may contribute to kidney function decline over time, and an observational study of 2,255 patients aged 60 to 80 after a heart attack found that higher protein intake was associated with faster kidney function decline. A position paper on protein needs in older people stated that older people with severe kidney disease (estimated GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) who are not on dialysis are an exception to its higher-intake advice and may need to limit protein intake. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
